sections.Aims and Fit of Module: Culture, Language and Community is designed to introduce Year 1 undergraduate students to questions of culture, language and community as global challenges. The module invites students to explore how cultural narratives, language use, identity, mobility and belonging shape human meaning, social participation, and the contexts in which contemporary academic, professional and creative activity take place. Drawing on three language and cultural traditions taught at the Modern Languages Centre — Spanish, Japanese and Chinese — the module offers students three structured cultural lenses through which to examine shared global themes such as migration, heritage, multilingualism, digital community, intercultural communication, and the cultural foundations of work and innovation. The module adopts a comparative cross-cultural framing in which the Chinese context functions both as the baseline cultural environment in which students live and study, and as one of three cultural traditions analyzed alongside the Hispanic and Japanese worlds. This positioning allows students whose backgrounds are Chinese, international, or both to engage in genuine intercultural reflection rather than treating any one culture as the implicit norm. The module is suitable for students considering future study in language-related, cultural, communication, business, social science or interdisciplinary humanities pathways, and equally for students from other disciplinary interests who need to understand how cultural and linguistic reasoning contributes to global problem-solving and to cross culture professional practice.
sections.Learning outcomes: A Examine how culture, language and community shape human meaning, social participation and contemporary global challenges, drawing on appropriate sources and evidence and acknowledging the perspectives and limits of those sources. B Compare how multiple cultural traditions frame shared challenges and identify points of convergence, difference and ethical complexity. C Communicate a cultural inquiry output and reflect on learning ownership, feedback use, teamwork and readiness for further academic study in light of the module experience.
sections.Method of teaching and learning: The module combines interactive seminars, guided inquiry workshops, applied cultural engagement activities, and reflective and project-based activities. Teaching is designed to support students in moving from broad curiosity and exploratory exposure towards more structured academic inquiry. The thirteen teaching weeks are organized in three cultural blocks (Spanish, Japanese, and Chinese), framed by an introductory phase and a synthesis-and-portfolio phase at the end. Each cultural block follows a recurring rhythm: a culture-and-language framing component, an applied cultural engagement component, and a comparative community-engagement discussion component. Applied cultural engagement activities may take a range of forms, including visits to local cultural sites, businesses, or community spaces; guest interventions from cultural practitioners; structured fieldwork tasks; analysis of authentic cultural artefacts; or curated immersive experiences delivered on or off campus. Students work individually and in groups to investigate a chosen cultural, linguistic or community-related challenge across the three traditions, developing evidence-informed interpretations and an accessible cultural inquiry output. All teaching is conducted in English. Selected source materials, examples and short authentic extracts may be drawn from Spanish, Japanese and Chinese, but no prior knowledge of any of these languages is assumed or required; the module is about cultures and communities in which these languages operate, rather than language acquisition.
